title: P0 hosted API prefix-hotspot + TTL drift incident diary
body:
Summary:

On 2026-01-28 we experienced a P0 production incident against the Hosted API that manifested as a correlated p95/p99 latency spike and a transient rise in 5xx responses for text-generation endpoints that use our KV cache prefixing. Total customer impact window: ~47 minutes (1120–1207 UTC). Severity: P0 (customer-facing latency / errors above SLO).

High level impact:
- p95 latency increased from ~160ms to ~1.2s for affected routes.
- 5xx rate for the route cluster jumped from 0.03% -> 3.8% at peak.
- ~4200 requests experienced partial streaming stalls requiring client reconnects.
- A subset of high-volume prefixes (approx 0.6% of prefixes) generated a disproportionate fraction of cache misses and lock contention.

Detection / Alerting:
- 11:18:48 UTC: synthetic canary alert (p95) fires for hosted-api-gen-eu-west.
- 11:19:05 UTC: oncall pager triggered for elevated 5xx error budget burn (SRE oncall: Ethan).
- 11:21:xx UTC: streaming session errors trend seen in observability dashboard (Liam joined).
- 11:30 UTC: incident declared P0.

Timeline (compressed):
- 11:12 UTC — first small uptick in p95 seen by internal dashboards (not alerted).
- 11:18:48 UTC — synthetic p95 alert fires.
- 11:20 UTC — initial triage: errors concentrated on prefix-sharded KV-backed model serving paths.
- 11:23 UTC — SRE looks at cache metrics: sudden increase in cache miss ratio for ~8 prefixes; high inflight lock wait for the prefix shards.
- 11:28 UTC — mitigation 1: throttle high-QPS prefixes at the edge (edge-ratelimit rule) to reduce write flood on the cache. Reduced incoming QPS by ~45% for top 3 prefixes; short term latency improves slightly.
- 11:34 UTC — mitigation 2: increase per-shard ephemeral worker pool (temporary), partially alleviates lock queue; however autoscaler oscillation causes thrash in some workers.
- 11:41 UTC — mitigation 3: rollback adaptive-batching rollout (v2) that was promoted earlier that morning to a canary subset; adaptive batching combined with cache-miss behavior was amplifying contention and causing larger delta in backend load per request. After rollback, p95 drops back toward baseline.
- 11:59 UTC — follow-up action: disable streaming-prefetch for affected model variant (reduced partial streaming stalls).
- 12:07 UTC — incident declared mitigated; monitoring onwatch.

Root cause hypothesis (multi-factor):
1) Prefix hotspot: a small number of prefixes experienced sudden QPS spikes (customer-driven traffic pattern; likely from a bot/test job) that caused disproportionate load concentrated on a handful of KV cache shards. Our prefix-sharding mapping placed these high-QPS prefixes on the same shard(s) which caused lock contention and long tail waits for KV operations.
2) TTL drift + aggressive rehydration: a recent change (config rollout 2026-01-26) reduced the TTL for cached prefixes under certain conditions to try to improve freshness. That shorter TTL caused synchronous rehydration bursts when a hot prefix expired across many nodes.
3) Adaptive batching interaction: the new adaptive-batching algorithm (canaryed 2026-01-28 03:00 UTC) increases batching size on lower latency signals — but when combined with sudden cache misses and longer KV latencies, a single request could hold resource slots longer and magnify queuing and timeouts. This interaction increased p95 and produced a small number of 5xx from timeout guards.
4) Autoscaler oscillation: attempts to scale ephemeral workers in response to the load spike were too coarse; scaling up and down over a short window caused resource churn and worsened tail latency for a short period.

Why prior mitigations didn't fully stop it:
- Edge throttles took ~5–7 minutes to propagate to all frontends (rule distribution).
- Our per-prefix surge protection thresholds were tuned for steady-state traffic, not for combined TTL rehydrate bursts.
- Adaptive-batching canary was active in ~12% of traffic and this path overlapped with the hot prefixes; we lacked a canary guard that would auto-disable adaptive-batching for prefixes experiencing cache miss storms.

Immediate mitigations (executed during incident):
- Apply emergency edge-rate-limits on top offending prefixes (manual rule) — reduced incoming delta quickly. Owner: eng-sre.
- Roll back adaptive-batching canary to previous stable version across all canary nodes. Owner: Marco Li.
- Increase per-shard ephemeral capacity and bump the lock wait timeout to reduce head-of-line blocking (temporary). Owner: Priya Shah.
- Disable streaming-prefetch for affected model variant to avoid partial stream stalls until KV latencies normalized. Owner: Liam O'Connor.

Post-incident action items (P0/P1 list, owners and deadlines):
- INF-692 (P1) — Add per-prefix surge detectors and automatic short-circuit to bypass batching when a prefix shows >X cache misses/min for Y min. Owner: Marco Li. Target: 2026-02-14.
- INF-701 (P0) — Rework TTL rehydration to use jittered staggered revalidation window per node and leader-election per shard to avoid synchronized rehydrates. Owner: Priya Shah. Target: 2026-02-07.
- INF-703 (P1) — Add canary guard in adaptive-batching: if KV latency > threshold or cache miss ratio climbs, throttle batching growth or disable for that prefix set. Owner: Ethan Brooks. Target: 2026-02-21.
- INF-710 (P1) — Improve autoscaler: faster warm-up + hold-minimum for bursty workloads; evaluate predictive scaling for known burst patterns. Owner: SRE infra team. Target: 2026-03-01.
- INF-717 (P1) — Dashboard and alerts: per-prefix cache-hit ratio, per-shard lock queue length, adaptive-batching impact panel. Create an automated runbook link in alerts. Owner: Observability. Target: 2026-02-04.
- INF-720 (P2) — Load-test harness: synthetic test that simulates TTL expiry storms across many nodes for a hot prefix to validate protections. Owner: Applied-ML infra. Target: 2026-03-15.

Runbook draft additions (quick patch notes for immediate inclusion):
- Detection: Alert when per-prefix request rate > 500 RPS AND prefix miss rate > 30% for 3 minutes.
- Triage checklist:
  1) Confirm prefixes affected via query logs (prefix histogram).
  2) Check KV shard mapping (which shards hold these prefixes).
  3) Examine per-shard lock_queue and inflight ops.
  4) If lock contention present -> apply per-prefix edge throttle (short-lived) and bump ephemeral workers.
  5) If TTL rehydrate detected -> temporarily increase TTL for the hot prefixes and stagger revalidation.
  6) If adaptive-batching is canaried and involved -> rollback canary.
  7) If autoscaler thrash observed -> hold current worker set and increase cooldown time.

Monitoring / SLO notes:
- We will add an SLI for "prefix-level tail latency" and include it in the error budget evaluation for text generation routes.
- Need an automated correlation between cache miss bursts and p95 spikes (simple rule-based detection for now).

Communications and customer follow-up:
- Customer-facing incident summary (short) to be prepared by CS after engineering review. Owner: Priya (draft due 2026-01-29).
- Internal all-hands: 2026-02-02 09:00 UTC for a walk-through with product, SRE, and applied-ML to explain mitigations and planned fixes.

Open questions / notes to self:
- Who kicked off the heavy traffic to those prefixes? We have a Linear ticket to correlate API keys and tokens to identify origin. This may be a legitimate customer test or an automated job.
- Can we add token-level soft-quota to prevent spikes from a single API key affecting other customers? This is a product/limits question.
- Check whether model upgrade earlier in the week changed timing of streaming-prefetch heuristics (might have increased cache-dependency).

Appendix: quick metrics snapshot at peak (11:25 UTC):
- Affected prefixes: 8 identified; combined QPS for these prefixes = ~1.9k (was normally 220–300).
- Cache miss rate for affected prefixes: 72% at peak (baseline ~12%).
- Per-shard lock queue length: median 1 -> 42+ for shard-3 at peak.
- Worker restart churn: 7 restarts across ephemeral pool in 4 minutes due to scale events.
- Error budget burn: 4.1% of daily error budget consumed in 45 minutes.

Quick retrospective thoughts (informal):
- Multi-factor incidents are noisy and often require a combination of fast manual mitigations plus longer-term architectural changes.
- Our prefix sharding is simple and performant for normal traffic; hotspots require smarter placement or hot-key isolation.
- Adaptive systems (batching, autoscaling) are powerful but create nonlinear interactions when cache behavior moves out of expected bounds — need better guardrails.

Next update plan:
- Update doc after the first 2 weeks of mitigation progress (stateful TTL rework PR and adaptive-batching guard implemented).
- Owner for this doc: Anita Patel (eng-sre).
